result.summary: Turnus insists on single combat with Æneas despite the pleas of Latinus and Amata. The truce is sworn but broken when Juturna stirs the Rutulians and Tolumnius throws a spear. Æneas is wounded and healed by Venus, Amata kills herself, and Æneas finally kills Turnus after seeing Pallas' belt.

scenes.title: Turnus insists on the duel
scenes.summary: Turnus demands the combat. Latinus and Amata plead with him in vain, and both champions arm.
scenes.stakes: Turnus risks his life and honour; Latinus and Amata fear losing their last hope and house.

scenes.title: The treaty is sworn
scenes.summary: Both armies mark out the lists and the leaders swear the treaty. Juno speaks to Juturna.
scenes.stakes: The peace and the fate of Latium and Troy depend on the oaths.

scenes.title: The truce is broken
scenes.summary: Juturna disguised as Camers stirs the Rutulians. After an omen Tolumnius throws a spear and battle erupts. Æneas is wounded and Turnus rages.
scenes.stakes: Æneas risks death by treachery; the truce and the peace are lost.

scenes.title: Venus heals Æneas
scenes.summary: Iapis cannot extract the arrow, so Venus heals Æneas with dittany. He returns to battle and the slaughter goes on.
scenes.stakes: Æneas's life and the Trojan cause.

scenes.title: Assault on the city
scenes.summary: Æneas attacks the town. Amata hangs herself, and Turnus, hearing of it, leaves Juturna to face Æneas.
scenes.stakes: The city's survival; Turnus's honour and life.

scenes.title: Duel and Jupiter's decree
scenes.summary: Turnus and Æneas fight, and Turnus's sword breaks. Juturna and Venus restore the weapons. Jupiter and Juno agree that the Latians keep their name and speech.
scenes.stakes: Turnus's life; Juno's hopes for Latium.

scenes.title: Death of Turnus
scenes.summary: A Fury drives Juturna away and unnerves Turnus. Æneas wounds him, and spares him until he sees Pallas' belt, then kills him.
scenes.stakes: Turnus's life; Æneas's mercy against vengeance.

characters.name: Tolumnius
characters.description: Rutulian augur who starts the fight

characters.name: Pallas
characters.description: Slain youth whose belt Turnus wears

characters.name: Faunus

alias_notes.explanation: Both names are used for Æneas's son.
Alternative name of the king of the gods.

notable_quotes.reason: Turnus admits that the gods, not Æneas, have defeated him.
Æneas kills Turnus in Pallas' name, ending the poem.

analysis.text: The final book sets mercy against vengeance, and fate against personal passion. Æneas's pietas gives way to grief for Pallas.
Jupiter's decree that the Latins keep their name and language reflects Roman pride in Italian identity merged with Trojan descent, in Augustus's time.

legacy.text: The abrupt ending, with the soul fleeing to the shades, has been much debated by readers and later poets, and Maffeo Vegio wrote a thirteenth book in 1428.

fun_facts.text: Virgil is said to have wanted the unfinished Æneid burned at his death in 19 BC; Augustus overruled him.

language_notes.text: "Punic land" means Carthaginian North Africa, a region famous in antiquity for lions.
"Turnus stops not the way": Turnus speaks of himself in the third person, saying he will not stand in the way of the duel.
"Dardan" means Trojan, from Dardanus, ancestor of the Trojan line; "Tartarus" is the deepest region of the underworld.
Latinus refers to oracles that Lavinia must marry a foreigner, so he could not give her to local suitors, including Turnus.
"May Fortune forefend the omen" is a formula to avert bad luck from the evil thing just spoken.
Aeneas's goddess-mother Venus rescued heroes in battle by hiding them in cloud, as she did Paris in the Iliad.
Orithyia was a wind-god's wife (Boreas carried her off), so her gift of horses explains their wind-like speed.
"Orichalc" is a bright, golden-looking metal, prized in ancient poetry.
"Emasculate Phrygian" is Turnus's insult: he mocks Aeneas and the Trojans as effeminate for their curled, perfumed hair.
The sun's steeds breathing radiance from their nostrils is the poetic image of sunrise: the sun-god's chariot rises out of the sea at dawn.
Vervain is a sacred herb used in religious ceremonies; the wreaths mark the attendants as ritual officials.
Juturna was loved by Jove, who made her a water goddess in return for taking her virginity. The 'odious bed' is Jove's, Juno's husband.
'Saturn's daughter' is Juno's epithet, since Saturn was her father. 'While yet on their lips' means the oaths have only just been spoken.
'Cognizance' means a distinguishing badge; the twelve rays on Latinus's brow mark his descent from the Sun.
Ascanius is the 'second hope of Rome' because he will carry on Æneas's line, from which Rome descends.
'Evander's town' is Pallanteum, the Arcadian settlement that allied with Æneas. 'Iulus' is another name for Ascanius.
Latona's twofold offspring are Apollo and Diana. Janus, the two-faced god, looks both ways, and Pluto rules the underworld.
The "fated band of Eturia" is the Etruscans (Tuscans), who had been told by an oracle to follow a foreign leader, Æneas, against Mezentius's supporters.
Jove's golden bird is the eagle, the bird sacred to Jove (the Greek Zeus) and a traditional omen-bringer.
Cornel is the cornel-wood spear; the wood stands for the weapon itself.
Falchion is a curved broadsword; "wildered" means bewildered.
Dolon, a Trojan spy, asked for Achilles' horses as his reward but was caught and killed by Diomed in the Iliad.
"Restiff" is an old form of restive, meaning unmanageable or refusing to obey the rider.
"Simples" are medicinal herbs; "virtue" here means healing power, not moral goodness.
Pæon was the physician of the gods in Homeric tradition; his name became linked with healing and with Apollo (Phœbus).
"Leech" is an old word for physician.
Dittany is a herb of Crete that ancient writers said drew out arrows and healed wounds.
Ambrosia is the food of the gods; panacea is a legendary all-healing herb.
"Ausonians" is a poetic name for the peoples of Italy, here Turnus' side.
"Rhœteian chief" means Æneas, a Trojan; Rhœteum was a Trojan headland.
"Duresse" means constraint or harsh treatment, here the trick played on him.
The "violated league" is the treaty between Trojans and Latins, broken earlier in Book 12.
Dardanus's sons means the Trojans, descendants of their founder Dardanus; Teucrians is another name for them.
Arcad means Arcadian; Evander's cavalry came from Arcadia in Greece.
'Reclaim the treaty fire in hand' means to avenge the broken treaty with torches; the treaty had been sworn with fire-lit sacrifice.
'Wildered' means bewildered; the citizens are thrown into confusion and divided.
Turnus's sister Juturna, a goddess, has taken the form of Metiscus, his charioteer, to protect him.
Drances is the Latian councillor who taunted Turnus with cowardice and urged peace with Æneas.
'Gentle powers of the grave' are the gods of the underworld, whom Turnus asks for kindness since heaven has abandoned him.
Saces rides with an arrow 'full in his face', meaning he is wounded in the face yet still gallops on.
"Expiate" means to atone for; Turnus offers to pay alone for the broken treaty by single combat.
Athos (a Macedonian mountain), Eryx (in Sicily) and the Apennine (Italy's mountain range) are named as the greatest of mountains to convey Æneas' vast size.
"Falchion" is a curved broadsword; here it is the sword Turnus inherited from his father.
"Guerdon" means reward or prize; the race is not a game but for Turnus' life.
The "Daunian goddess" is Juturna, Turnus' sister, daughter of Daunus; she had earlier disguised herself as his charioteer Metiscus.
Jupiter refers to Juno's admission that fate has destined Æneas for heaven.
Swearing by the river Styx was the gods' most binding oath, which even Jupiter could not break.
Jupiter and Juno are both children of Saturn, so she is his sister as well as his wife.
Tartarean: of Tartarus, the deepest region of the underworld. Megæra is one of the three Furies, here said to be born of Night.
Parthians and Cydonians (from Crete) were famed archers; poisoned arrows were associated with them.
Jove had taken Juturna's virginity and made her immortal, as compensation. She now bitterly regrets this gift.
The river of her deity: Juturna is a water nymph, so she sinks into her own stream, the Tiber's waters.
Boundary stones were sacred markers. The remark that men are puny 'now-a-days' recalls Homer's heroes who far exceeded later men.
Ausonians: an old name for the peoples of Italy. Daunus is Turnus' father.
The soul flies 'to the shades' meaning the underworld; the line repeats the ending of the Iliad's Hector death formula.

context_notes.text: Latinus is king of Latium. Daunus, Turnus's father, ruled the Rutulians, and Latinus here offers Turnus other brides.
Amata is Latinus's wife and Lavinia's mother. She had favoured Turnus as her daughter's husband throughout the war.
The Fire-god is Vulcan, divine smith, who also made Aeneas's armour.
Aeneas wears the armour Venus obtained from Vulcan, described earlier in the poem.
Alban Mount is the hill near Rome later famous for the cult of Jupiter Latiaris. Virgil notes that it had no fame yet.
Æneas's shield and armour were forged by Vulcan, and the shield shows scenes of Rome's future history.
Salted barley (mola salsa) was sprinkled on sacrificial victims, and libations of wine were poured from dishes.
The Rutulians are Turnus's people. They doubt the fairness of the duel because Æneas is the stronger fighter.
Juturna is Turnus' sister, a water nymph. She has been sent by Jove's queen's will to prolong the war and save her brother, so she disguises herself.
An augur interpreted omens, especially bird signs, so Tolumnius' reading of the eagle carries religious authority.
Mars (the Greek Ares) was the god of war, associated with Thrace, which lies by the river Hebrus.
Iapis was a healer favoured by Apollo (Phœbus), who also presided over prophecy, music and archery.
Hector, Trojan prince killed by Achilles, was Æneas' kinsman, here called Ascanius' uncle.
Juturna is Turnus' sister, a nymph; she disguises herself as his charioteer to keep him from Æneas.
Æneas's beauteous mother is Venus, who protects her son and prompts this strategy.
Amata is Latinus's queen, who favoured Turnus as son-in-law and opposed Æneas; she believes Turnus dead.
Lavinia is the daughter of Latinus and Amata, and the bride for whom Turnus and Æneas contend.
Jupiter's scales weigh the fates of the two fighters, a motif also found in Homer's Iliad.
Æneas' armour was made by Vulcan, god of the forge, so Turnus' ordinary borrowed sword shatters against it.
Faunus was an old Italian god of the countryside; Laurentian refers to Laurentum, in Latium.
Venus is Æneas' mother and protects him, so she answers Juturna's help by returning his spear.
The Alban kings and the Roman stock look ahead to the founding of Alba Longa and Rome, descended from Æneas' people.
The sire is Jove, who has just agreed with Juno that Turnus must now face his fate.
The Fury becomes an owl-like bird, a creature of ill omen to Romans.
Anchises, Æneas' father, is old and far away in the story's past; Turnus appeals to Æneas' filial piety.
Pallas, young son of the ally Evander, was killed by Turnus, who took his sword belt as a trophy.

literary_notes.text: Comparing Turnus to a wounded lion shows his rage growing from the injury to his pride.
Latinus's counsel is a "healing hand" that only inflames the wound, making Turnus's fury worse.
Ivory stained with purple and lilies mixed with roses paint Lavinia's blush through colour imagery.
Turnus addresses his spear as a living comrade, showing his trust in arms and his heroic confidence.
The bull butting a tree compares Turnus's pre-battle rage to an animal's, echoing the earlier lion image.
The shift to the present tense (moves, pours) makes the armies' march vivid and immediate.
Messapus is called 'tamer of horses', a stock Homeric-style label, and his descent from Neptune links him to the sea god.
Juno's admission that Turnus faces a mightier destiny hints that he will lose the duel.
Calling Æneas the 'parent stock of the Roman tree' is a metaphor that looks ahead to Rome's future glory.
Latinus compares his unbroken oath to the sceptre, which can never grow leaves again. It is ironic because the treaty will in fact be broken.
Turnus's downcast look, pallor and quiet step show his doubt and foreshadow his defeat.
The repeated "plunges among the ranks" frames her disguise and conveys the swift, deliberate action of her intervention.
The eagle and swan scene is a symbolic portent, which Juturna uses to turn the Italians' minds toward war.
Death is presented as iron slumber and everlasting night, softening the violence into a solemn image.
Æneas appears bareheaded and unarmed, pleading for the truce, which shows his piety and respect for the treaty.
Turnus is compared to Mars driving his steeds amid Terror, Wrath and Treachery, exalting his fury and making him seem godlike.
Turnus' advance is likened to the north wind driving waves and clouds, showing how irresistibly the ranks scatter before him.
Fortune and Phœbus are imagined as patrons who withhold help, showing the failure of human skill.
The human healer admits his own helplessness and credits divine power, which also signals Æneas' destined role.
Æneas' advice to Ascanius shows his sense of duty and the value of example, with a notable admission about luck.
Æneas' advance is likened to a storm that terrifies farmers before it arrives, stressing its inevitable destructive force.
Juturna darting about is compared to a swallow in a rich man's house, a small domestic image against the war.
The poet calls on a god to help him recount the slaughter, a traditional epic invocation.
Paired fires and rivers present Æneas and Turnus as equal natural forces on a collision course.
The panicked citizens are compared to bees smoked out of a rock, their noise and confusion vividly conveyed through the extended image.
'An iron harvest of naked blades' pictures bristling swords as a crop, while war 'ebbing' from Turnus's field makes battle a tide.
Turnus's mix of shame, grief and wrath, shown in a list of surging emotions, reveals his pride and passion as he faces fate.
Turnus's acceptance that Fate is too strong marks his turning point and foreshadows his duel and death.
The falling rock, sweeping away trees, herds and men, conveys Turnus' destructive, unstoppable rush.
The fighting bulls, with herds watching to see which becomes leader, compare the heroes' duel to a contest for dominion.
The sword is called "faithless" as if it betrayed Turnus by choice.
The hound and stag make Æneas the hunter and Turnus the prey, with the near-bite showing the narrow gap between them.
The wood's "fangs" make the olive root seem a living thing resisting Æneas, as if Faunus protects Turnus.
Jupiter smiles and teases Juno's rage, lightening the scene while he still firmly decides the outcome.
The Fury's swift, deadly descent is compared to a poisoned arrow, stressing speed and incurable harm.
Turnus' paralysis is compared to a nightmare in which effort fails, conveying helplessness against divine will.
Comparing the spear's roar to siege engines and thunderbolts magnifies Æneas' power.
Just as mercy seems likely, the belt Turnus wore in triumph turns the moment, showing pride's consequences.
The doubled name 'Pallas, Pallas' presents the dead youth as the true avenger, giving the killing a moral justification.
